patch.value:
Found while fixing the same defect in two packages on the same day (`pm-rl`, `pm-vcs`).

## The gap

`--date` documents its default as *"resolved tag date when available, otherwise current UTC date"*. That fallback is correct for a package on its way to a release, and wrong for a package that is deliberately held back.

A release-gated package has **no tags by construction**. So the fallback fires on every generation, and the committed heading records *the day it was generated* rather than any property of the release. `--check` compares against a freshly generated heading, so it agrees only on the day of generation and fails every day after — with no change to the tracker and none to the code.

Both affected packages had already passed CI and been reviewed; the check simply started failing the next morning. `pm-vcs` had an item closed explicitly claiming its release gate had been made deterministic. It had not been — the UTC fix addressed timezone drift, which is a different axis from clock dependence.

## Why the current workaround is a trap

The only fix available today is `--date <fixed>`, which is an unconditional **override**, not a fallback. So the moment the package is actually released and tagged, that pin silently wins over the real tag date and the heading is wrong in a new way. The fix for today's problem becomes tomorrow's.

Both packages now carry `--date 2026-07-31` / `--date 2026-07-30` in three scripts each, and every one of those has to be removed by hand at release time. Nothing enforces that.

## Suggested resolution

A fallback-shaped flag rather than an override — something like `--date-fallback <date>`, used only when no tag resolves, so the tag keeps priority the moment one exists and the pin disarms itself.

A stronger variant worth considering: this fleet uses CalVer, where the version *is* the date (`2026.7.29` → `2026-07-29`). An option to derive the fallback from the version — `--date-from-version` — would need no per-release maintenance at all and would make the heading self-consistent by construction. Every released package in the fleet already follows that pairing; today it holds by convention rather than by anything enforced.

Either would remove the whole class: the heading would stop depending on when the command runs, without introducing a pin that has to be remembered later.
